overview: This file consists of ten consecutive Department of State “List of Papers” or cross-reference sheets for the Petroleum—Japan portion of decimal file 894.6363, chiefly covering 1940–1943. The entries trace Japanese efforts to secure petroleum, aviation gasoline, lubricants, fuel oil, synthetic fuels, refining equipment, and related technology from the United States, Latin America, China, Southeast Asia, and the Soviet Union; the activities of Standard-Vacuum, Mitsui, Mitsubishi, and other firms; and the development of American export licensing, asset-freezing, and economic-warfare policies. Later sheets shift from commercial reporting and contractual disputes to wartime intelligence about Japanese production, tankers, refineries, captured oil regions, and alternative fuels. The sheets also document the circulation of information among the State, Treasury, Justice, Navy, and Commerce Departments, Congress, oil companies, and American diplomatic posts.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: entries 340–343
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State filing staff
subfiles.about: Index entries concerning Japanese oil development, gasoline contracts, petroleum sales, and restrictions on American products in North China.
subfiles.summary: The sheet records correspondence with Standard-Vacuum about Japanese oil development and North China trade, a conversation between Secretary Hull and the Japanese ambassador about a disputed gasoline contract, and a report on Japan's petroleum-sales monopoly. It also cross-references information about restrictions on American petroleum products at Fengzhen, Suiyuan, Kalgan, Baoding, and elsewhere in northern China.

subfiles.title: Sheet 61: entries 344–348
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State filing staff
subfiles.about: Index entries on Japanese petroleum activity in North China and Mexico, oil statistics, large shipments, and artificial petroleum production.
subfiles.summary: This sheet points to Grew's report enclosing a Standard-Vacuum account of Japanese petroleum activity in North China and to Justice Department information on large shipments and possible subversive activity. It also indexes reports on Japanese oil dealings in Mexico, national production and consumption statistics, synthetic-petroleum development, and state petroleum distribution.

subfiles.title: Sheet 62: entries 353–361
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State filing staff
subfiles.about: Index entries on Japanese corporate attempts to obtain gasoline technology, equipment, drums, and large petroleum shipments from the Americas.
subfiles.summary: The entries describe Mitsubishi and Nippon Soda representatives seeking American sources of high-grade gasoline and oil-rig equipment, congressional inquiries into gasoline and million-ton oil shipments, and a proposed Colombian shipment of aviation gasoline in steel drums. Other entries concern Standard-Vacuum's proposed sale of its Bitumula shares, Japanese exchange-control obstruction, Japanese petroleum output, and State Department investigations of Davis and Company shipments.

subfiles.title: Page 63: entries 362–367
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State filing staff
subfiles.about: Index entries on Japanese Army gasoline inquiries, American export controls, corporate negotiations, and Japan's motor-fuel problem.
subfiles.summary: This sheet records a Japanese Army inquiry to Standard-Vacuum for monthly gasoline deliveries in China, private reports on Japan's petroleum position, and replies to senators about restrictions under the presidential proclamation of July 26, 1940. It also covers negotiations involving Standard-Vacuum, Shell, Socony-Vacuum, and Mitsui; difficulties selling American shares in Bitumula; and a translated Dutch consular report on Japanese motor-fuel problems.

subfiles.title: Sheet 64: entries 368–373
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State filing staff
subfiles.about: Index entries on Allied oil policy, Japanese purchasing behavior, commercial arrangements, naval fuel inquiries, and possible Japanese purchases in Peru.
subfiles.summary: The sheet indexes British statements on raw-material shipments to Japan, Walden's account of Japanese reluctance to contract beyond March 31, and Hornbeck's suggestion that oil companies accept arrangements while later finding delivery difficult. It also covers litigation between Universal Oil Products and Japan Gasoline, a Japanese Navy fuel-oil inquiry reported by California Texas Oil, and investigations into possible purchases or surveys of Peruvian oil resources.

subfiles.title: Page 65: entries 374–382
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State filing staff
subfiles.about: Index entries on fusel-oil shipments, export restrictions, Southeast Asian petroleum stocks, lubricants, and suspected equipment transshipment to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The entries include Grew's follow-up on Japanese oil supply, statistics showing unusually large American fusel-oil exports, and memoranda on British policy and petroleum stocks in Thailand that might support a Japanese advance toward Singapore. They also index discussions of Far Eastern petroleum exports, restrictions on lubricating oil aboard a Japanese freighter, Standard-Vacuum's request for policy guidance, and suspected movement of oil-field machinery through Laredo to Japan.

subfiles.title: Page 66: entries 383–391
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State filing staff
subfiles.about: Index entries on Japan's oil position, shipments, remittances, licensing policy, and company assets under American freezing controls.
subfiles.summary: This sheet lists Navy and Treasury reports on Japan's economic and petroleum situation and future shipments from Port San Luis, together with Standard-Vacuum material on shipments and Japanese imports from 1929 through 1940. Several Hiss memoranda examine remittances, the relationship between export and payment licenses, Dutch consultations, and Standard-Vacuum stock in Shanghai. A Treasury entry records Nishiyama's proposal for paying for pending oil shipments.

subfiles.title: Page 67: entries 392–399
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State filing staff
subfiles.about: Index entries on Japanese industrial intelligence, naval fuel deliveries, corporate balances, and oil imported before the freezing regulations.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to Justice Department intelligence on Japanese government activity in industry and commerce and to a naval report on fuel-oil deliveries to Japanese ships. Several entries concern money owed by Mitsui to General Petroleum, conversations involving Socony-Vacuum representatives, and the treatment of oil imported before the American freezing regulations. It closes with further Justice Department reporting on the Japanese oil situation.

subfiles.title: Page 68: entries 401–410
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State filing staff
subfiles.about: Index entries on wartime estimates of Japanese oil production, refineries and tankers, Soviet supply allegations, and petroleum-export statistics.
subfiles.summary: The entries begin with requests for Soviet information on synthetic-fuel production in the Japanese Empire and reports prepared for British economic-warfare authorities. They include Thornburg's assessment of Japan's oil position, intelligence on Japanese and enemy-controlled tankers and refineries, a petroleum-industry prospectus, and export statistics for 1931–1941. Later correspondence addresses Senator Maloney's allegation that the Soviet Union was diverting Lend-Lease petroleum to Japan and reports from Switzerland on Japanese production.

subfiles.title: Page 69: entries 411–414
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State filing staff
subfiles.about: Index entries on Japanese alternative-fuel claims and intelligence concerning demolished oil fields and refineries in Southeast Asia.
subfiles.summary: The sheet records a press claim that the Japanese could produce crude oil and gasoline from cottonseed oil and a request concerning the German oil position. It then indexes reports on the demolition of oil fields and refineries in the Netherlands East Indies and South Sumatra, analysis of Japanese gasoline recovered in a floating drum, and interpretation of serial photographs of destroyed petroleum installations.

interest: These sheets provide a compact chronological map of the transformation of petroleum from a commercial and diplomatic issue into a central instrument of wartime economic policy. They are especially useful for tracing how company intelligence, consular reporting, congressional pressure, export licensing, payment controls, and military analysis interacted before and after the freezing of Japanese assets. The many references to particular contracts, cargoes, firms, intermediaries, and foreign oil regions offer historians precise leads to fuller documents elsewhere in the decimal files, while the abrupt shift toward synthetic fuels, tanker intelligence, demolished Southeast Asian refineries, and aerial photography reveals the changing informational needs of the United States after the outbreak of war.
